approved: Export Market Development Grants Amendment Bill 2013

Moved the Export Market Development Grants Amendment Bill 2013, proposing to focus the scheme on small exporters to East Asian, frontier and emerging markets, increase grants there from seven to eight, reduce grants to the United States, Canada, United Kingdom and European Union from seven to five, and deliver annual savings of $25 million.

Moved an amendment on the Export Market Development Grants Amendment Bill 2013, supporting its passage while condemning the $25 million annual reduction, increased red tape and alleged budget mismanagement, and promising a review of the changes if elected.

Supported the Export Market Development Grants Amendment Bill 2013, arguing that its changes would focus assistance on emerging Asian markets, save $25 million per annum and ensure public funds supported eligible small and medium businesses prudently.

Supported the amendment, arguing that the bill's $25 million annual saving would weaken exporters, particularly small Western Australian businesses and agricultural producers, and calling for stronger Austrade support and market access.

Argued that difficult conditions for farmers and regional communities made export assistance important, criticised the government's live cattle trade decision, and urged stronger trading ties with Indonesia and support for Australian farm exports.

Argued that the bill's $25 million annual saving was a cut that would hurt exporters, farmers and regional communities, while criticising reduced support for established markets and broader government trade and water policies.

Supported amendments to the Export Market Development Grants Amendment Bill 2013, arguing that excluding major markets while adding one East Asian grant year confirmed broken promises and reduced funding to $125 million, the lowest level in decades.

Opposed the government's third major change to the Export Market Development Grants scheme since 2007, saying it will cut $25 million to cap funding at $125 million, favouring grants to East Asian and emerging markets over traditional markets such as the United States and Europe.

Argued the EMDG changes will harm Australia's business events sector, citing a convention bureau estimate that international events won in 2011 to 2012 delivered $385.2 million in economic benefit, and said tourism generates $94 billion a year in spending, arguing the government should have reviewed the scheme with industry before cutting $25 million from it.

Supported the shadow minister's criticism of the EMDG changes, arguing they will not improve access to Asia but simply save the government $25 million annually, and said Australia's damaged relationship with Indonesia, worth only $11 billion in two-way trade compared with $15 billion with New Zealand, reflects the government's mishandling of live animal exports and other issues.

Opposed removing event promoters from the EMDG scheme, warning this would hurt companies like Brisbane Marketing that help attract international conferences, cited a convention bureau estimate of $385.2 million in economic benefit from events won in 2011 to 2012, and said the $25 million funding cut would damage Queensland's export industries.

Argued that the Export Market Development Grants Amendment Bill 2013 appropriately refocused support toward East Asian, emerging and frontier markets, increased available grants from seven to eight, reduced grants for established markets from seven to five, generated annual savings of $25 million, and provided reimbursements of up to $150,000.

The Export Market Development Grants Amendment Bill 2013 was introduced to concentrate the EMDG scheme on small businesses exporting to East Asian and frontier/emerging markets, saving $25 million annually by increasing grants to those markets from seven to eight while reducing grants to the US, Canada, the UK and the EU from seven to five, effective 1 July 2013.
